scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Waka Waka originated in the Andean highlands, with Bolivian researchers tracing it to Umala in La Paz and Peruvian researchers to Ácora in Puno.
It evolved from the agricultural use of oxen (ttinti wacas) to a satirical representation of Spanish bullfighting introduced during colonial times.
The dance reflects the cultural fusion of indigenous and Spanish elements, symbolizing cattle work and bullfighting.
on_screen: Map: Bolivia, Peru · South America
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Waka Waka is performed during major Andean festivals: the Oruro Carnival and Gran Poder festival in Bolivia, and the Fiesta de la Virgen de la Candelaria and Virgen del Carmen in Peru.
It satirizes Spanish bullfighting while celebrating cattle and agricultural traditions.
The dance embodies cultural identity, history, and social commentary through its characters and choreography.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Women dancers wear more than 16 colorful layered skirts called polleras, an alpaca mantilla covering the head, and embroidered jubón jackets.
Men wear bull costumes made from dried and shaped animal skins with bells hanging from the bulls' necks.
The dance is performed in urban and rural settings, notably during festivals such as the Oruro Carnival and Gran Poder in Bolivia, and the Virgen de la Candelaria in Peru.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Characters in the dance include the torero (bullfighter), bulls, lecheras or polleronas (milkmaids with many skirts), kusillos (young jesters), jilakatas (older dancers), and camaleros negros (carriers with swords).
These roles animate the dance's narrative and social satire.
Variants include Waka Tinti from Cairiri, Tinti Caballo, and Waka Tinki from Paxsiamaya in Bolivia.
Waka Waka descends from indigenous agricultural dances involving oxen and was transformed by Spanish colonial influences, especially bullfighting.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Waka Waka is sibling of Tinku: Another Bolivian folk dance with indigenous roots and festive character.
Waka Waka is sibling of Diablada: Also performed at Oruro Carnival, shares Andean cultural context.
Waka Waka is influence of Caporales: Modern Bolivian dance influenced by traditional dances including Waka Waka.
